props.title: How to become an AI Engineer in 6 months (RESOURCES)
props.thesis: Ronin proposes six months of building with existing models, from Python foundations to deployed applications. The goal is practical ability, not senior expertise.
props.take: Build, test, deploy, and publish one project monthly; show working demonstrations.

phases.label: Month one
phases.line: Practice Python with CS50P, use Git, and build FastAPI endpoints.

phases.label: Month two
phases.line: Use OpenAI, Anthropic, and Instructor; validate outputs and restrict tool permissions.

phases.label: Month three
phases.line: Build retrieval with LlamaIndex and Chroma; test cited answers across ten to twenty files.

phases.label: Month four
phases.line: Build controlled agents before LangGraph; test twenty to fifty cases with DeepEval.

phases.label: Month five
phases.line: Deploy with Docker Compose; add authentication, Celery queues, and Langfuse tracking.

phases.label: Month six
phases.line: Choose products, applied engineering, or automation; demonstrate usable work.

props.title: how to master AI in 30 days (the exact roadmap)
props.thesis: Machina proposes a month of practice, moving from fundamentals to connected workflows. Reusable knowledge environments matter more than collecting prompts.
props.take: Build one task-specific Claude Project with relevant documents and clear instructions.

phases.label: Model basics
phases.line: Compare settings and verify claims before trusting fluent answers.

phases.label: Tool choices
phases.line: Machina favors Claude, Gemini 3 Pro, and Grok for different tasks.

phases.label: Context design
phases.line: Set instructions; write, select, compress, and isolate reference material.

phases.label: Creative direction
phases.line: Specify scenes clearly; budget repeated attempts for short video shots.

phases.label: Build and automate
phases.line: Connect Claude Code, n8n, and external tools.

phases.label: Grounded answers
phases.line: Use NotebookLM or retrieve relevant passages; errors remain possible.

phases.label: Careful integration
phases.line: Test models through OpenRouter; Clawdbot still needs technical setup.

props.title: 20 AI Concepts You Must Understand in 2026
props.thesis: Rahul connects twenty AI concepts to practical choices about instructions, model adaptation, retrieval, and tools.
props.take: Choose the intervention your problem needs, and verify factual answers.

points.label: How models work
points.line: Models learn connection strengths, then predict the next fragment of text.

points.label: Reliable instructions
points.line: Supply context, examples, output formats, and manageable steps; verify answers.

points.label: Specialization
points.line: Continue training on focused material, and use human rankings to guide responses.

points.label: Lower costs
points.line: LoRA trains small additions. Quantization reduces precision and storage.

points.label: Retrieval and action
points.line: Search documents before answering, or connect tools through repeated action and observation.

points.label: Beyond text
points.line: Image generation removes noise progressively; Rahul also discusses Sora and Runway.

props.title: You can go from zero to hireable AI engineer in 4 months. Here's the
props.thesis: AI Guides proposes four months of project-led preparation using existing models. The plan assumes fifteen to twenty hours weekly and does not guarantee employment.
props.take: Publish a Python project, then advance through working milestones instead of tutorials.

phases.label: Practice first
phases.line: Build independently for thirty minutes per study hour; publish your work.

phases.label: Foundations
phases.line: Learn Python and supporting skills; build a utility handling files and errors.

phases.label: Integration
phases.line: Compare five prompts; build an invoice parser with enforced output structure.

phases.label: Resilience
phases.line: Manage history, streamed responses, costs, retries, and tool permissions.

phases.label: Retrieval
phases.line: Build cited answers from documents; inspect retrieved passages before changing models.

phases.label: Agent judgment
phases.line: Build a three-tool loop before LangGraph; test twenty to thirty representative inputs.

phases.label: Portfolio
phases.line: Deploy three projects with Docker, spending caps, and Langfuse traces.

props.title: Become AI Agentic Engineer in 6 Weeks (Full Course) - Part 1
props.thesis: Rahul argues that reliable agents need more than frameworks: model behavior must be surrounded by evidence, code-enforced rules, and stage-level measurement.
props.take: Retrieve evidence, enforce rules in code, and measure each stage before changing models.

points.label: Six weeks
points.line: Progress from foundations through prompting, tools, memory, production, evaluation, and security.

points.label: Probability
points.line: Likely text is not necessarily true; less randomness cannot fix factual errors.

points.label: Validate and ground
points.line: Backend code checks eligibility; retrieved policy meets live order details.

points.label: Context
points.line: The example totals ninety-seven thousand two hundred tokens; select relevant information.

points.label: Latency
points.line: Streaming reveals output sooner but does not accelerate input processing.

points.label: Measurement
points.line: Illustrative perfect retrieval still ends at eighty-five percent final accuracy.

props.title: How to Become a Graph Architect With Zero Experience (Full Course)
props.thesis: CyrilXBT argues that connected facts and explicit agent controls belong together. A documented, tested project demonstrates competence better than credentials.
props.take: Deepen one domain project; document sources, failures, changes, and retest outcomes.

phases.label: Foundations
phases.line: Weeks one and two: map relationships manually across twenty support tickets.

phases.label: Extraction
phases.line: Weeks three and four: Extract, Resolve, Assemble, Query; test matches and retain sources.

phases.label: Agent control
phases.line: Weeks five and six: lock plans, separate execution and recovery, and bound retries.

phases.label: Portfolio
phases.line: Weeks seven through ten: join documents and agents; publish design choices and failures.

phases.label: Resources
phases.line: Claude Cookbook, Andreas Kollegger's DeepLearning.AI course, and an agent-design paper.

phases.label: Learning evidence
phases.line: Keep dated failures, changes, and retests; deepen one domain project.

props.title: From 0 to Graph Engineer: The 14-Step Roadmap Using Kimi K3 (Full
props.thesis: Al-Awady argues that relationship-heavy questions need connected facts, not similarity alone. Engineers must control structure, identity, evidence, and maintenance.
props.take: Prove your validation pipeline before scaling extraction.

phases.label: Foundations
phases.line: Practice Cypher in Neo4j until you can follow three connected relationships.

phases.label: Design first
phases.line: Use ten to fifteen real questions; include source references and validity windows.

phases.label: Resolve identities
phases.line: Compare surrounding sentences; send uncertain name matches for human review.

phases.label: Construct carefully
phases.line: Extract explicit facts; carry canonical names; automate repairs and budget limits.

phases.label: Validate first
phases.line: Check structure, exact quotations, domain rules, and human samples before writes.

phases.label: Analyze and retrieve
phases.line: Consider lighter GraphRAG options; route questions to graphs, vectors, or SQL.

phases.label: Operate responsibly
phases.line: Update sources, preserve conflicts, track staleness; save K3 for difficult work.

props.title: AI Agents: The Complete Course
props.thesis: Rahul argues that reliable agents need bounded workflows, measurable steps, and operational safeguards before greater autonomy.
props.take: Build a bounded sequential workflow; expand autonomy only after failures become diagnosable.

points.label: Bounded iteration
points.line: Limit tool choices within repeated reasoning, action, and observation.

points.label: Explicit context
points.line: Provide background, tools, and references; separate checkable tasks and memory.

points.label: Completion checks
points.line: Evaluate components and outputs; apply scoring, format checks, and human approval.

points.label: Sequential coordination
points.line: Start with ordered specialists; reserve parallel work for independent tasks.

points.label: Quality before speed
points.line: Fix retrieval, prompts and models first; then track spend, tokens and wins.

points.label: Contained execution
points.line: Use disposable Docker containers, resource limits, and sensitive-output scanning.

props.title: Become AI Agentic Engineer in 6 Weeks (Full Course) - Part 2
props.thesis: Part two moves from prompting to security: the model proposes an action, and deterministic backend checks decide whether it may actually run.
props.take: Assume the model can be fooled — enforce permissions in the backend, not the prompt.

nodes.label: Label the source
nodes.sub: Mark retrieved pages, emails and issues as untrusted data

nodes.label: Authenticate
nodes.sub: Identify the real requester before any tool is offered

nodes.label: Authorize
nodes.sub: Derive allowed tools from that person's own permissions

nodes.label: Validate the call
nodes.sub: Check ownership, eligibility, prior refunds and the limit

nodes.label: Gate and log
nodes.sub: Human approval for money and deletion, then audit

props.note: Search the web, read internal documents and send email in one session, and you have built an exfiltration path.

props.title: The 25 AI Concepts You Actually Need to Understand in 2026
props.thesis: Kanika sorts twenty-five concepts into layers, and argues that real expertise comes from connecting the mechanisms rather than collecting the vocabulary.
props.take: Build one small workflow on a real bottleneck, with retrieval, evals and cost limits.

layers.label: Computational basics
layers.line: Tokens, context windows, embeddings, and training versus inference

layers.label: Model capabilities
layers.line: Match capability, latency and cost — bigger is not automatically better

layers.label: Beyond prompting
layers.line: Agents plan and act; function calling reaches APIs, code and databases

layers.label: Grounded workflows
layers.line: Retrieve, summarise, draft, review, publish — a process, not a chatbot

layers.label: Reliability and value
layers.line: Evals, guardrails, human review, and cost control as usage grows

props.heading: What all ten roadmaps agree on
items: Build end-to-end apps on existing models — do not train from scratch
Python, APIs and backend basics come before any model theory
Prompting, structured outputs and tool calling are the core loop
Add retrieval only when the model needs facts it cannot hold
Agents are the frontier, and graphs are how the newest guides frame them
Ship and deploy publicly — every roadmap ends at a portfolio, not a certificate
props.closer: The timelines are marketing. The syllabus underneath is remarkably consistent.

items.title: Top fifty Claude skills and repos

props.title: The AI Engineering Skills Map
props.thesis: Ng argues AI engineering is becoming a capability every developer needs, resting on four connected areas rather than on one job title.
props.take: Audit yourself across all four areas, not just prompting and code generation.

points.label: Built on evidence
points.line: Drawn from over ten thousand job postings, plus interviews with experts and hiring managers.

points.label: Engineer the uncertainty
points.line: You cannot know the output in advance, so measure it — evals and repeated error analysis.

points.label: Fundamentals still rule
points.line: Cost, scalability, reliability, security: the tradeoffs an agent cannot weigh for you.

points.label: Steer the agent
points.line: Manage context, judge when to step in, and give agents verifiers to check their own work.

points.label: Coordinate safely
points.line: Know when a spec is needed, and stop agents from damaging a production database.

points.label: Decide what gets built
points.line: As agents implement specs, engineers move upstream into product judgment.

props.title: AI Engineering Skills Map: Building and Deploying AI Applications
props.thesis: The second map names six competencies for building reliable applications out of components whose output you cannot predict in advance.
props.take: Let evaluation and error analysis pick your next move — Ng calls it the deciding skill.

points.label: Know the model
points.line: Tokenisation, context, caching, cutoffs, sampling and tool calling all shape the design.

points.label: Ground it in data
points.line: Vector indexes, knowledge graphs or a semantic layer — match retrieval to the data.

points.label: Design the execution
points.line: A fixed sequence, or a harness that picks its next action; plus sandboxing and memory.

points.label: Let evals steer
points.line: Inspect traces, analyse errors, then choose measures — and evaluate the evaluators.

points.label: Operate under drift
points.line: Monitor real usage, watch for prompt injection, match testing to the consequences.

points.label: Keep the ML basics
points.line: Supervised and reinforcement learning, bias and variance, still earn their place.

props.title: AI Engineering Skills Map: Using coding agents
props.thesis: Ng's third map is about steering coding agents, and he is blunt that longer unattended runs are not the goal.
props.take: Set verifiable goals, keep the context current, and intervene by risk — not by vibe.

phases.label: Plan
phases.line: Research, explore the codebase, then write a spec and an execution plan

phases.label: Execute
phases.line: Build and verify together, in steps whose results you can check

phases.label: Operate
phases.line: Release gates, log inspection, and a route back to earlier phases

phases.label: Calibrate autonomy
phases.line: Collaborate, delegate, or let it retry — decide by risk and cost

phases.label: Verify the verifier
phases.line: Automated checks stop agents, but their criteria need scrutiny too

phases.label: Hold the context
phases.line: AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, hooks, retrospectives, clearing agent debt

items: Fifteen of the hundred articles, covered end to end
Ten roadmaps that disagree on time and agree on content
Build on existing models; learn the plumbing first
Prompt, structure the output, call the tool — that is the loop
Retrieval when facts are missing; agents when steps are needed
Andrew Ng's skills map is about judgment, not tools
The big skill lists are inventory — useful, but not a curriculum
props.closer: The roadmaps get you started. The tool layer is where the work actually happens.

Someone collected the hundred best applied A I
articles on X.

Roadmaps, skill maps, agent harnesses, retrieval,
inference, evals. Together
they are over three hundred thousand words.
This series reads all of them, so you don't
have to. We start where everybody starts —
with the learning paths.
Chapter one. Learning paths and skill maps.

Ten of the most-shared roadmaps for breaking into
applied A I.
Here is what chapter one covers.
Two long-form roadmaps open it — six months
to A I engineer, and thirty days
to a working foundation. Then two concept maps, one
with twenty ideas, one with twenty-five.

A four-month path to being hireable. A two-part
agentic

engineering course. And three guides to graph
engineering, which
is the newest of these tracks.

They disagree about timelines. They agree almost
completely about
content. Watch for that pattern as we go.
Ronin lays out a six-month route into practical AI

engineering. He emphasizes building products with
existing models rather

than training enormous models yourself. The goal is
working
ability, not instant seniority.

Month one starts with Python practice through CS50P,
alongside
Git and basic web skills. Build a small script,

then create FastAPI endpoints that check incoming
data. Month

two introduces OpenAI and Anthropic, with Instructor
helping enforce

predictable output formats. Tool calling means
models request actions
while your code executes them.

Validate results, limit permissions, and account for
conversation history,

retries, and costs. Month three covers retrieval,
meaning finding
relevant source material before answering.

Use LlamaIndex and Chroma, then test cited answers
across

ten to twenty files. Check missing context before
blaming

the model. Month four adds agents, systems that
choose

actions as tasks unfold. Build one directly before
adopting

LangGraph, and limit its steps and retries. Test
twenty
to fifty representative cases with DeepEval.

Month five makes deployment concrete through Docker
Compose, authentication,

and Celery background queues. Track prompts, delays,
and costs

with Langfuse. Month six branches into products,
applied engineering,

or automation. Ship usable projects, or build
Temporal workflows
with approvals and audit trails.

Build, test, deploy, and publish one project
monthly. Use
working demonstrations when pursuing opportunities.

Can thirty days build practical AI skills? Machina
proposes

two to three hours daily, prioritizing reusable
workflows over prompt collections.

Model basics come first: compare settings and verify
claims

rather than trusting confident language. Tool
choices follow

the author's preferences, not independently
established rankings. Claude handles

coding, Gemini 3 Pro supports research, and Grok
tracks

X activity. Context design means arranging
information the model can use.

Claude Projects

Custom

before

Rahul connects twenty AI concepts to everyday
engineering decisions.

His argument is practical: understanding mechanisms
helps you choose
the right intervention.

Foundations begin with models learning connection
strengths and interpreting

text fragments through surrounding words. Model
behavior follows

from predicting what text comes next across vast
training

collections. Available context is limited, and
fluent answers can

still contain invented facts. Reliable instructions
supply context, examples,

output formats, and manageable steps for the model.
Rahul

Specialization means continuing training

Human rankings can separately guide models toward

additions while leaving the original model

the model

Weaviate, or pgvector. Tool-using systems repeatedly

Retrieve changing facts, adapt

ambitious

Behind Rahul's six-week agent course sits a warning
about

require dependable software
around unpredictable text generation.

Six weeks span foundations, prompting, tools,

not truth. Reducing

SQL or Elasticsearch can provide information

remains

Predictable dependencies need

Context is the information supplied with a request,
including

history and documents. Rahul's example reaches

hundred tokens, the small text units models process.

Select relevant material instead of filling every
available space

with documents. Latency includes processing input
before generating output,

Trim history

and tool definitions, and reuse cached prefixes
where appropriate.

Measurement must separate retrieval, interpretation,
and final answers. His

Retrieve evidence, enforce rules, and measure each

since Edwin Aldrin and Buzz Aldrin name one person.

Explain failures, including confident answers caused

graph engineering

relationship-heavy questions
need connected facts, not similarity alone.

Foundations means learning graphs, networks of

across runs. Contained execution uses disposable
Docker containers

Rahul's second part is about security.
The idea is simple. A tool-using agent turns text
into real actions. So the backend must decide what
runs, not the prompt. Start by labelling the source.

Direct injection arrives in user input. Indirect
injection hides
inside a retrieved page, an email, or a GitHub
issue. An issue asking your coding agent to delete
authentication tests is data, not an instruction.

Then authenticate. Identify the real requester
before offering any
tool. Then authorize. Derive the allowed tools

from that person's own permissions. Rahul calls the
failure
a confused deputy. Alice reads Bob's salary because
the agent's credentials were wider than hers.
Then validate the call itself. For a refund, check

ownership, earlier refunds, eligibility and the
amount. Permission
to refund an order does not justify five hundred
thousand dollars on a forty-nine dollar purchase.

Finally, gate and log. Require human approval for
money

and deletion. And watch tool combinations, not
single tools.

Search the web, read internal documents, and send
email

in one session, and you have built an exfiltration
path.

Design the permissions assuming the model can be
fooled.

His closing exercises are worth doing. Design a

And validate a transfer whose amount does not match

Kanika's map covers twenty-five concepts, and it is
built in layers.
At the base are the computational basics. Tokens
are the pieces a model processes. They set your
cost, your latency, and how much fits

in the context window. Embeddings turn meaning into
numbers,

so you can search by similarity. Training adjusts
parameters.
Inference just uses them.

Above that sit model capabilities. Seven billion,
seventy billion,

four hundred and five billion. Those numbers
describe scale,
not suitability. Match capability, speed and cost
to the job.

The third layer goes beyond prompting. Agents plan,
then

act. Function calling reaches APIs, code and
databases. Orchestration
coordinates models, people and approvals. Her point

is that workflow structure matters more than clever
wording.

The fourth layer is grounded workflows. Retrieval
pulls

in real material before the model answers. Her
example

runs retrieve, summarise, draft, review, publish.
That
is a process, not a chatbot.
The top layer is reliability and value. A plausible

falsehood still needs verifying. Evaluation measures
accuracy, relevance, safety

and usefulness. Guardrails limit sensitive data and
unauthorized actions.

And compounding systems feed experience back into
better prompts
and better retrieval.
And her advice is to start small,
on a bottleneck that actually matters.
So what did ten roadmaps actually agree on?

Build on existing models instead of training your
own.

Learn Python, A P Is and backend basics before model
theory.
Treat prompting, structured outputs and tool calling
as the core loop. Add retrieval only when
the model needs facts it cannot hold. Then move

to agents, which the newest guides describe as
graphs.
And every single one ends the same way —
with something shipped and public.

The timelines are marketing. Thirty days, six weeks,
four

months, six months. The syllabus underneath barely
changes.
Chapter two. Skills, tools, and M C P.
Where the roadmaps end, the tooling begins.
Chapter two runs to fifteen articles. We cover
the first five here.
Three of them are Andrew Ng's skills map, published
in parts — the single most shared item
in the whole collection.
Between them sit two very large lists of Claude

skills and repositories. One promises fifty. The
other promises sixty-seven.
Ng's pieces are about judgment. The lists are about
inventory. You need both, and it helps to know
which one you are reading.
This is the single most shared article
in the whole collection.
Andrew Ng's claim is that A I engineering
is no longer a specialty. It is becoming something
every developer needs. And he built the map
from evidence — over ten thousand job postings, plus
interviews with experts and hiring managers.

The first area is engineering around uncertainty.
You cannot
know an A I output in advance. So you

measure it instead. That means evaluations and
repeated error
analysis, not hope.

The second is plain software fundamentals. Cost,
scalability, reliability,

security. Ng warns that an inexperienced developer
will accept
a bad decision from an agent without noticing
it. You need the vocabulary to steer.
The third is using coding agents well. Manage
the context. Judge when to intervene. Give the agent
a verifier so it can check its own work.

And coordinate several agents without damaging a
production database.
The fourth is product judgment. As agents get better

at implementing a specification, engineers move
upstream into deciding
what should be built at all.

Four areas. Most people only audit themselves on
one.

And underneath all four, Ng puts continuous
learning.
The practices are changing too fast to freeze what
you know today.
This is a catalogue, not a comparison. Worth knowing
before you read it.

The author sorts fifty tools into three layers.
Skills

supply procedure. M C P supplies access.
Repositories supply
the engine that runs things.

In the skills layer, Superpowers bundles test-driven
development, debugging

and planning. Systematic Debugging insists you find
the cause

before changing code. Skill Creator turns a workflow
you

describe into a skill file. File Search combines
ripgrep
and a s t-grep. Context Optimization is about token
spend and cache behaviour.

In the access layer, three picks. Tavily does
search,

extract, crawl and map. Context7 pulls in current
library

documentation on request. Task Master turns a
product document
into dependency-linked tasks.

In the engine layer, LangGraph expresses agents as
graphs.
CrewAI organises them by role and goal. Ollama runs

models locally. And promptfoo tests prompts and
security before you ship.

The repository watchlist goes further. Parallel
coding with cmux

and claude-squad. Persistent memory. Test-first
enforcement through T D
D Guard. And tracing for agent runs.
Installing is just copying a skill folder into your
Claude skills directory, then restarting.
One honest note. The author explicitly asks you
to run your own security check. Treat
this as a shortlist, not an endorsement.
Ng's second map is narrower. It is about building
and deploying the application itself.

Six competencies. The first is knowing the model.
Tokenisation,

context allocation, cache behaviour, knowledge
cutoffs, sampling settings, tool
calling. All of them change your design. Fine-tuning

and self-hosting are specialist options, not
substitutes for understanding.
The second is grounding in data. Decide what belongs
in the prompt and what the model should go
and fetch. Match the retrieval to the shape
of your data. A vector index, a knowledge graph,

or a semantic layer over structured records. Convert
your
PDFs, HTML and images into usable inputs, and keep
those pipelines fresh.

The third is designing execution. Either a fixed
sequence
of calls, or a harness where the model repeatedly

picks its next action. Then sandboxing, memory, and
guardrails.
The fourth is the one Ng singles out. Disciplined

evaluation and error analysis. He calls it the
strongest

skill separating A I builders. Inspect the traces.
Find
the errors. Then choose what to measure. And check
your evaluators too.
He adds that the right approach shifts
with the project and its maturity.

Fifth, operate under drift and prompt injection.
Sixth, keep
the machine learning basics.

Prompting alone was never going to deliver
reliability.

Sixty-seven skills, and a headline that promises a
whole development team.

Set the promise aside. The mechanism underneath is
genuinely
useful. A skill is a folder. It holds instructions,

examples, constraints, and sometimes scripts. That
is what makes
a workflow survive between sessions.
The author suggests a staged order. Start by making
skills. Skill Creator turns your bullet points into
a draft. You then run a handful of test
prompts, and fix whatever fails.

Next, planning. Grill Me interrogates your
requirements, including data
models and failure cases. Write a P R D

combines an interview with codebase exploration. P R
D
to Plan sequences thin vertical slices. P R D
to Issues turns them into assignable work.

Then engineering discipline. Test-driven
development. Systematic debugging — reproduce,
isolate, one fix, verify.

Then repository safety, which is the part people
skip.

Git Guardrails adds hooks that block push, hard
reset

and clean before they run. Pre-commit assembles
linting, type
checks and tests.

Beyond code, the list reaches further. A
documentation generator

derives OpenAPI material straight from your routes.
Theme Factory

turns a brand description into palette tokens. An
Excel
server drives spreadsheets without desktop Excel.
Judge any of these on the tasks you actually
fail. Not on the headline.
The third map is the one most people need,
and it ends on a warning.

Ng's process has three phases. Plan. Execute.
Operate. Planning

means research, codebase exploration, and a
specification covering requirements,

design and architecture. Execution pairs building
with testing. Operating
adds release gates and log inspection. And a failed
check sends you back a phase.

How much planning? That depends. A throwaway
prototype needs

a sentence. An established product serving real
users deserves
a checked specification.

Then calibrate autonomy. Work alongside the agent,
delegate
a chunk, or let it retry toward a clear
goal. Decide by risk and cost, not by habit.

Then verify the verifier. Automated checks tell an
agent

when to stop. But the criteria themselves need
scrutiny,
and sometimes a human still has to look.

Then hold the context. An agents file records
architecture

and conventions. Hooks trigger reviews.
Retrospectives capture lessons.
And you clear the debt the agents generate.

Ng names the warning signs too. Overengineering.
Missing verification.
Stopping too early. And destructive actions.
He also says to learn how the harness itself
works. How it retrieves code, how it manages
the context window, how it spawns subagents.

His closing warning is direct. Social media
exaggerates how

useful those hours-long, million-token runs really
are.
That is the first fifteen articles.

Ten roadmaps that argue about timelines and agree
about

substance. Five tooling pieces that split cleanly
into judgment and inventory.

The through-line is simple. Learn the plumbing,
build

on models that already exist, and ship something
people can open.

Everything after this — context, memory, harnesses,
retrieval, inference,
evals — assumes you have done that part.
